sweep_summary: The only title-works with stress in the title for Old Spanish (Glottolog 597174, Harrington, Fletcher & Beckman 2000 on accent articulation in Australian English) is a Glottolog machine mis-tag ('computerized assignment from "conflicts"', verified on the downloaded Glottolog record) and is irrelevant; priority none. The catalog's deciding source (Menéndez Pidal 1904 Manual §5-6, pp. 22-25) was re-downloaded from archive.org and the catalog quote verified verbatim; the 1925 5th edition already held by the project says the same. Two further open first-hand sources were downloaded and read this search of works with stress in the title: Hanssen 1913 Gramática histórica Cap. V §§39-46 (pp. 16-18), whose 'Regla Fundamental' — the accent stays on the syllable it occupied in Latin, exceptions listed — independently confirms the 'lexical' coding; and Menéndez Pidal 1908 Cantar de Mio Cid vol. I Gramática §§29-31 (pp. 166-169), the only source here specifically about the Old Spanish period, which confirms inheritance and refines with period facts (reína, treínta, veínte not yet shifted; ámen oxytone until the 15th c.). No source contradicts the catalog; nothing remains unread or to be acquired.org's search API and direct downloads only.

new_statements.quote: 39. Regla Fundamental. El acento queda en la sílaba en la cual se halla en latín: fraxinum > fresno, civitatem > ciudad. Las excepciones provienen de ciertos accidentes que pertenecen en parte á la gramática latina y en parte á la castellana. [...] 40. [...] El acento latino carga en la penúltima sílaba si ésta es larga, y en la antepenúltima si la penúltima es breve. Consonantes combinadas alargan la sílaba: paréntes. Se exceptúan las consonantes combinadas con r: íntegrum, álacrem, cólubram, ténebras. Pero, en el latín vulgar, también éstas alargan la sílaba y atraen el acento [...] Así se explica el acento de las palabras castellanas entero, alegre, culebra, tinieblas.
new_statements.translation: 39. Fundamental rule. The accent stays on the syllable on which it stands in Latin: fraxinum > fresno, civitatem > ciudad. The exceptions come from certain accidents belonging partly to Latin grammar and partly to Castilian grammar. [...] 40. [...] The Latin accent falls on the penultimate syllable if it is long, and on the antepenultimate if the penult is short. Consonant clusters lengthen the syllable: paréntes. Clusters with r are excepted: íntegrum, álacrem, cólubram, ténebras. But in Vulgar Latin these too lengthen the syllable and attract the accent [...] This explains the accent of the Castilian words entero, alegre, culebra, tinieblas.
new_statements.citation: Hanssen, Federico. 1913. Gramática histórica de la lengua castellana. Halle a. S.: Max Niemeyer. Cap. V El Acento, §39-40, pp. 16-17.
new_statements.locator: Segunda Parte, Fonología, Cap. V El Acento, §39 'Regla Fundamental' p. 16 and §40 pp. 16-17 (djvu lines 1191-1212)
new_statements.reading: Word-stress position in (Old and Modern) Spanish is the Latin accent position carried over unchanged, with listed exceptions (Vulgar-Latin muta-cum-liquida, hiatus-to-diphthong shifts, recomposition, Greek loans, analogy, later vowel contraction). Since Latin quantity is gone, the position is a lexical property of each word (mostly paroxytone, always within the last three syllables), not derivable synchronically — exactly the catalog's 'lexical' coding. An independent second author (Hanssen) states this as the 'fundamental rule', corroborating Menéndez Pidal; and Menéndez Pidal's 1908 Cid grammar §§29-31 adds Old-Spanish-period specifics (reína, treínta, veínte still with classical accent; ámen oxytone to the 15th c.).

Old/Modern Spanish word stress = the Latin accent position inherited word by word (Hanssen 1913 §39 'Regla Fundamental', p. 16; Menéndez Pidal 1904 §5, pp. 22-23), with all the listed exceptions being diachronic relocations (muta cum liquida, hiatus>diphthong, recomposition, Greek loans, analogy, contraction); no synchronic phonological rule places stress, so it is a lexical property within the final three syllables. new_statements.quote: Most lexical items retained the stress on the vowel on which it had fallen in Latin. No word of two or more syllables in Latin carried stress on the final syllable. Consequently, in medieval Hispano-Romance, word-final stress was very rare, limited for the most part to infinitives [...], suffix-stressed verb endings [...], to nouns that had lost -e after a coronal consonant (e.g., PANEM > pan 'bread', RATIONEM > razón, SENIOREM > señor 'lord'), and later to Arabisms ending in -í [...]. Penultimate stress is by far the prevalent pattern in the medieval language. Prior to the massive influx of Latinisms into the written language in the second half of the fifteenth century, examples of words with antepenultimate stress were rare

Consequently, in medieval Hispano-Romance, word-final stress was very rare, limited for the most part to infinitives (-ARE > -ar, -ERE > -er, -IRE > -ir), suffix-stressed verb endings (preterit -é, -í, -ó, future -é, -ás, -á, -án), to nouns that had lost -e…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Hanssen/Menéndez Pidal statement (stress remains where Latin had it, lexical, mostly paroxytone, within the last three syllables); adds the distributional detail that final stress is rare and morphologically restricted, that antepenults were rare before the 15th-century Latinisms, and the Old-Spanish-specific final-stressed items alguién and peró.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on one of the last three syllables and stays on the vowel that bore the Latin accent, so its position is a lexical inheritance rather than a synchronic rule; penultimate stress is by far the dominant pattern, final stress is rare and confined to infinitives, suffix-stressed verb endings (preterit -é, -í, -ó; future -é, -ás, -á, -án), apocopated nouns (pan, razón, señor) and Arabisms in -í (rubí, alfaquí, baladí), and antepenultimate stress was rare before the 15th-century wave of Latinisms.
new_statements.exceptions: Latin proparoxytones became paroxytones by loss of the post-tonic vowel (CALIDUM > caldo, DUBITA > dubda, COMITEM > cuende, HOMINEM > omne); rare native proparoxytones águila, áspero, húmido, rávano, cuévano, búsqueda, pérdida (n. 9: only águila, áspero, pérdida frequent); medieval alguién stressed on the last syllable, unlike modern alguien (p. 41); medieval peró final-stressed after PER HOC, later shifted to initial syllable in proclitic use (p. 92 n. 29); reína, veínte still trisyllabic with hiatus through the 14th century (p. 21).
new_statements.identity_note: Dworkin describes 'medieval Hispano-Romance', i.e. Castilian-centred Old Spanish of roughly the 13th to 15th centuries, with occasional Leonese and Aragonese asides; the alguién and peró remarks are explicitly about the medieval language as opposed to modern Spanish.

sources.note: §5 'Acento clásico conservado en romance' (pp. 22-24): the accent stays on the same syllable from Plautus through Cervantes to today; Latin put it on the penult when long by nature or position, else on the antepenult; §6 lists Vulgar-Latin deviations (positio debilis: entero, tinieblas; hiatus-to-diphthong shift: mujer, pared; prefixed verbs: reniego). The catalog quote is verbatim from this text (scanned 'Planto' = Plauto). Coding 'lexical' stands.

sources.quote: 29. El acento se conserva: 1] En voces latinas: astil, huebos, etc. Acento del latín vulgar entergar, alegre, mugier. [...] 30. En el caso de encuentro de dos vocales, ocurren cambios de acento para convertir el hiato en diptongo. 1] El castellano antiguo abunda en formas dobles, de las cuales el castellano moderno olvidó ó la de hiato ó la de diptongo. [...] 2] No habían aún dislocado su acento reyna; así «reynas» es consonante de «finas» [...] También los numerales treynta, *veynte responden á la acentuación clásica; son trisílabos

sources.note: Gramática, Vocales: Acento §§29-31 (pp. 166-169), on the language of the Cantar (12th-13th c.) specifically. §29: the accent is preserved — in Latin words (astil, huebos), with the Vulgar-Latin accent in entergar, alegre, mugier; Greek words keep Greek accent (Éremus > yermo, Isidorus > Esidro) except -ia words (ecclesia > eglesia). §30 'Dislocación del acento': on hiatus, the accent shifts to make a diphthong, Old Castilian having doublets (Dí-os bisyllabic beside Dios; imperfects in -ié; fui/fue); and, refining the catalog for the old stage, forms not yet shifted: reína (rhymes with finas),…
